blocks.text: Newton's second law states that when a force acts on a body it produces acceleration in the same direction. A force acting on a moving body along the direction of its velocity changes the magnitude of the velocity (speed), keeping the direction unchanged. On the other hand, a constant force acting perpendicular to the velocity of a body moving in a circular path changes the direction but the magnitude of the velocity (speed) remains the same. Such a force makes the body move in a circle by producing a radial (or centripetal) acceleration and is called the centripetal (centre-seeking) force. Fig. 3.6a shows a ball tied to the end of a string whirled in a horizontal surface; it would not continue in a circular path if the string snapped: when the string snaps while the ball is at point A (Fig. 3.6b), the ball follows the straight-line path AB, the tangent at A. In circular motion the direction of motion changes continuously (Do You Know).

Thus a force is needed to change the direction of the velocity continuously at each point of circular motion with uniform speed. The force that does not alter speed but only direction at each point is a perpendicular force acting along the radius of the circular path; it always pulls the object towards the centre, and its direction is perpendicular to the tangential velocity at each point.

blocks.title: Centripetal force
blocks.text: The force needed to bend the straight path of a particle into a circular path is called the centripetal force. For a body of mass m moving with velocity v in a circular path of radius r, Fc = m a_c = m v^2 / r ... (3.12), where a_c = v^2/r is the centripetal acceleration, directed towards the centre of the circle. As v = r omega, Fc = m r omega^2 ... (3.13).

blocks.title: Example 3.2
blocks.text: If a CD of diameter 12 cm spins at 210 rpm, what is the radial acceleration of a point on its outer rim? Solution: convert 210 rpm into a frequency in revolutions per second: f = 210 rev/min x (1/60) min/s = 3.5 rev/s = 3.5 Hz. For each revolution the CD turns through 2 pi radians, so omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 3.5 rev/s = 7.0 pi rad s^-1. The radial acceleration is a = omega^2 r = (7.0 pi rad s^-1)^2 x 0.06 m = 29 m s^-2.

blocks.title: Example 3.3
blocks.text: A ball tied to the end of a string is swung in a vertical circle of radius r under gravity (Fig. 3.7). What is the tension in the string when the ball is at the top point A of the path and its speed is v there? Solution: for the ball to travel in a circle the force acting on it must provide the required centripetal force. At A two forces act on the ball, the pull of the string T and its weight w; both act along the radius at A, so their vector sum must furnish the centripetal force: T + w = m v^2 / r, and as w = mg, T = m v^2 / r - mg = m (v^2/r - g). If v^2/r = g, T is zero and the centripetal force is just equal to the weight.
In every circular or orbital motion a centripetal force is needed, provided by some agency:

items: When a ball is whirled in a horizontal circle by a string, the tension in the string provides the necessary centripetal force.
For an object placed on a turntable, friction is the centripetal force.
The gravitational force is the cause of the Earth orbiting the Sun, and of the Moon and artificial satellites revolving around the Earth.
A normal (perpendicular) magnetic force compels a charged particle moving along a straight path into a circular path.

When a vehicle takes a turn on a road it also needs a centripetal force, provided by the friction between the tyres and the road. If the road is slippery, then at high speed the friction may not be sufficient to provide the necessary centripetal force; the vehicle cannot take the turn and may skid or even topple. To overcome this difficulty the highway is banked on turns: the outer edge of the track is kept slightly higher than the inner edge. Banked tracks are needed for turns taken so quickly that friction alone cannot provide the centripetal force (Tid-bits).

blocks.caption: Centripetal force, artificial satellites, weightlessness and artificial gravity (original diagram after Figures 3.6 to 3.14 and topics 3.2 and 3.3).
blocks.long_description: A body moving in a circle is pulled towards the centre by a force equal to its mass times the square of its speed over the radius, or its mass times the radius times the square of its angular velocity; this force changes only the direction of motion, and without it the body flies off along the tangent. The force is supplied by a string's tension, by friction on a turntable or between tyres and road, by gravity for planets and satellites, or by a magnetic force on a moving charge, and it is exploited in the centrifuge, the washing-machine dryer and the cream separator. For a satellite gravity supplies it, so near the Earth the orbital speed is the root of g times the Earth's radius, about seven point nine kilometres per second with a period of about eighty-four minutes, and farther out the speed is the root of the gravitational constant times the Earth's mass over the orbit radius. Because gravity alone provides the centripetal force, nothing inside the satellite needs a supporting force, so everything appears weightless; spinning a wheel-shaped ship so that the rim's centripetal acceleration equals g restores an artificial gravity.

blocks.text: An object moves in a circle because of centripetal force; if the magnitude of the applied force falls short of the required centripetal force, the object moves away from the centre of the circle. The centrifuge (Fig. 3.8a) works on this principle.

blocks.caption: Applications
rows: one of the most useful laboratory devices; a mixture is rotated at high speed for a specific time to separate denser and lighter particles; in sample tubes the denser particles settle at the bottom and the lighter rise to the top (Fig. 3.8b)

a long cylinder with hundreds of small holes in its wall; wet clothes are piled in and the cylinder rotated rapidly about its axis; water moves outward to the walls and drains out through the holes, so the clothes dry quickly (Fig. 3.9)

milk, a mixture of light and heavy particles, is whirled rapidly; the light particles gather near the axis of rotation while the heavy particles go outwards, so the cream is easily separated from the milk (Fig. 3.10)

blocks.prompt: A string 0.5 m long can withstand a maximum tension of 35.6 N. Find the maximum speed at which a 0.5 kg stone can be whirled with it in a vertical circle (numerical problem 3.4). Why is it harder for a car to turn at higher speed, and why do we tumble on a sharp fast turn (short question 3.5, constructed response 3.3)?
blocks.explanation: The tension is greatest at the bottom of the circle, where T - mg = m v^2 / r, so 35.6 - 0.5 x 9.8 = 0.5 v^2 / 0.5, giving v^2 = 30.7 and v = 5.5 m s^-1. The centripetal force m v^2 / r grows with the square of the speed, so at higher speed the friction between tyres and road may not be enough and the car skids; our bodies tend to keep moving in a straight line (inertia) while the vehicle turns, so we lean outward and may tumble.

items: A perpendicular force changes only the direction of velocity: centripetal force Fc = m v^2 / r = m r omega^2, along the radius towards the centre; without it the body goes off along the tangent. Top of a vertical circle: T = m (v^2/r - g).

Supplied by string tension, friction (turntable, tyres), gravity (orbits), magnetic force; banked roads on fast turns. Applications: centrifuge, washing-machine dryer, cream separator. Example 3.2: 29 m s^-2.
